strengths: Pairmixer offers a simple, practically meaningful architectural contribution: removing triangle attention and sequence updates from an AlphaFold3-style backbone while retaining triangle multiplication substantially reduces computation.

The controlled comparisons against a retrained Pairformer are unusually extensive, covering three model scales, matched training budgets, learning curves, inference scaling, and both RCSB and CASP15 benchmarks.

On the main RCSB evaluation, the large model essentially matches Pairformer across folding, protein-protein docking, and protein-ligand metrics while using 269 rather than 421 GPU-days; inference speedups grow to approximately 4x at 2,048 tokens.
The paper includes useful ablations of mixer type, triangle-multiplication width, FFN width, and diffusion depth, along with FLOP calculations and reasonably comprehensive hyperparameters.
The method is clearly motivated and presented, and improving the efficiency of repeated structure prediction has substantial relevance to screening and biomolecular design.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the method primarily removes components from an established architecture, while triangle-multiplication-only processing already appears in related structure models. The paper does not provide a formal expressivity or approximation result supporting the claimed equivalence to triangle attention.

Generalization evidence is mixed. On CASP15, the large Pairmixer is consistently below the matched Pairformer on several metrics, especially protein-protein docking, while docking and ligand subsets contain only 12-14 examples. Thus, claims of broadly matching Pairformer are somewhat overstated.

The binder-design evaluation establishes runtime and memory improvements but not design quality: it provides only one qualitative example, without quantitative structural confidence, interface metrics, diversity, sequence plausibility, experimental validation, or comparisons on standardized design benchmarks.

Table 1 appears to reverse the Pairmixer and Pairformer runtime columns: every displayed Pairmixer time is larger despite the reported 2.0-2.6x Pairmixer speedup. This directly obscures evidence for a prominent downstream claim.

Dataset counts are inconsistent or insufficiently explained: the RCSB set is described as containing 533 structures, Figure 6 reports 538, and Table 4 reports 539; interaction subset sizes also differ substantially between Figure 6 and Table 4. Comparisons imported from prior literature may not use fully harmonized inference and ranking protocols.

The low-norm dropout experiment does not establish that triangle multiplication learns sparse interactions: deleting already low-magnitude terms is expected to have limited effect, and no compute-efficient sparse implementation or comparison with attention patterns is demonstrated.

Architecture results appear to come from single training runs despite small metric differences, and uncertainty is not reported for the central matched Pairmixer-versus-Pairformer comparisons. Runtime methodology also omits details such as precision, compilation, warm-up, and variance.

No code, trained checkpoint, or release commitment is stated, limiting reproducibility given the very large training budget. Overall, the efficiency result is compelling enough for a marginal accept, but reporting inconsistencies and incomplete validation prevent a stronger score.

strengths: Pairmixer is a simple, practically relevant simplification of the Boltz-1/Pairformer backbone: retaining pair representations and triangle multiplication while removing attention reduces computational cost without materially degrading performance on the main RCSB benchmark.

The experiments are unusually compute-intensive and include three model scales, training trajectories, FLOP accounting, runtime scaling with sequence length, and comparisons under a largely shared Boltz-1 pipeline.
The reported efficiency improvements are substantial: approximately 34% fewer GPU-days at the largest scale and increasing inference speedups for long sequences.
The paper includes useful architectural ablations and an exploratory analysis of triangle-multiplication sparsity.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is limited. The primary contribution is removal of existing Pairformer components, while prior work already uses triangle-multiplication-centric or attention-free biomolecular backbones. The paper lacks direct experimental comparisons with the closest simplified architectures, such as MiniFold.

The evidence does not support the broad claim that Pairmixer matches Pairformer across benchmarks. On CASP15, the large Pairmixer is consistently worse than the matched Pairformer, especially for DockQ and ligand metrics; several subsets contain only 12–14 examples, yielding weak statistical evidence.

Evaluation protocols and sample counts are inconsistent or insufficiently explained. The RCSB set is variously reported as 533, 538, or 539 complexes, while interaction subsets also differ substantially between Figure 6 and Table 4. Comparisons to prior systems are imported from the literature, with unclear protocol alignment.

Most main results use oracle selection over five poses. Pairmixer has no confidence model, so its reported top-1 result is merely the first sample. This leaves practical ranked-prediction quality inadequately evaluated and makes system-level comparisons difficult to interpret.

The binder-design claims are unsupported. The evaluation demonstrates runtime and memory differences but provides only one qualitative structural example, with no quantitative design-quality metrics, independent structure validation, sequence-quality analysis, experimental validation, or success-rate comparison.

Table 1 appears to reverse the Pairmixer and Pairformer runtime columns: every displayed Pairmixer time is larger despite the stated 2–2.6x speedup. Other inconsistencies include a 73.3% RMSD win rate in Figure 7 versus 74.7% in the text and incorrect figure/table references. These errors reduce confidence in the reporting.

The efficiency study omits uncertainty over runtime measurements, detailed peak-memory measurements, and sufficiently controlled hardware/software benchmarking information. Claims about memory scaling rely on a few selected binder-design targets rather than systematic curves.

The low-norm dropout experiment does not establish that triangle multiplication learns attention-like sparse interactions: deleting already small-magnitude terms is naturally less disruptive, and random dropout is not magnitude-matched. The Match3 experiment is small, achieves modest accuracy, and does not cleanly isolate representation order from architectural differences.

No controlled ablation separately quantifies removing sequence attention, triangle attention in the backbone, and triangle attention in the MSA module. Consequently, the experiments do not precisely establish which simplification produces the reported efficiency-quality tradeoff.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of an explicit code/checkpoint release and incomplete operational details for dataset construction, filtering, runtime measurement, and external-baseline evaluation. The paper also lacks discussion of biosafety or dual-use considerations associated with scalable binder design.

strengths: Pairmixer is a simple, practically meaningful simplification of an AlphaFold3-style backbone: removing triangle and sequence attention while retaining triangle multiplication substantially reduces compute without sacrificing RCSB accuracy.

The evaluation is unusually compute-intensive and includes retrained Pairformer and sequence-only Transformer controls at three model scales. On the RCSB benchmark, the large Pairmixer essentially matches Pairformer across folding, protein–protein docking, and protein–ligand docking while using about 34% fewer GPU-days.

The efficiency gains are compelling: inference is reported as 1.6× faster at 512 tokens, 2× at 1024 tokens, and 4× at 2048 tokens. The BoltzDesign integration further demonstrates relevance to an important downstream workload.

Ablations comparing triangle multiplication with FFT, pooling, and one-directional mixing help establish that the particular pairwise operation matters. The inference-time sparsification analysis and Match3 experiment offer useful, albeit preliminary, mechanistic insight.

weaknesses: The novelty is primarily architectural deletion rather than a fundamentally new operation: triangle-multiplication-only architectures have substantial precedent. The strongest contribution is therefore the empirical demonstration at AlphaFold3-style cofolding scale, and the paper should position itself accordingly.

Generalization evidence is mixed. On CASP15, Pairmixer is often below the matched Pairformer, particularly for interaction metrics; for example, the large phase-2 model obtains DockQ success of 0.52 versus 0.64 and mean lDDT-PLI of 0.34 versus 0.36. The public Boltz-1 checkpoint is stronger still on several ligand metrics. This qualifies the broad claim that Pairmixer simply matches Pairformer.

The binder-design section establishes speed and OOM limits but not design quality. Its quality evidence consists only of qualitative structures, without standard in-silico design metrics, experimental validation, diversity analysis, or success rates. Claims about generating high-quality or comparable binders are consequently under-supported.

The memory-efficiency claim lacks controlled peak-memory measurements across sequence lengths. OOM thresholds in one downstream pipeline are useful but confound backbone memory with the rest of that pipeline.

Some comparisons are difficult to audit. System-level results are taken from prior literature, sample counts differ from the paper's retrained-model tables, and Pairmixer lacks a confidence model, so its reported “top-1” is merely the first sample rather than confidence-ranked output. The text also inconsistently describes this comparison as an average across poses.
Table 1 appears to have the Pairmixer and Pairformer runtime columns reversed: its numerical entries make the nominal Pairmixer slower, contradicting both the reported speedups and surrounding text.

Reproducibility is only moderate despite good hyperparameter reporting: the manuscript does not provide a code or checkpoint release commitment, and runtime methodology omits details such as precision, compilation, synchronization, warm-up, and variability. The very high training cost makes independent reproduction especially difficult.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, practically significant replacement for the costly Pairformer backbone: retaining triangle multiplication and pairwise feed-forward layers while removing triangle attention and sequence updates.

The controlled comparison is unusually extensive. Pairmixer and a retrained Pairformer are evaluated across three model scales, training checkpoints, recycling settings, and multiple biomolecular modalities while largely keeping the surrounding Boltz-1 system fixed.

The main efficiency result is compelling: Pairmixer uses about 34% fewer GPU-days at large scale and provides 1.6× to 4× inference speedups, with larger gains on long sequences, while remaining close to Pairformer on the principal RCSB metrics.

The evaluation covers RCSB, CASP15, PoseBusters, antibody-antigen, protein-nucleic-acid, and RNA benchmarks. Distogram evaluation and stratification by sequence length and MSA depth help establish that the diffusion decoder or favorable examples do not fully explain the results.

The ablations are informative: they study component removal, mixer alternatives, triangle-multiplication and FFN widths, recycling, and sparsification behavior. The Match3 experiment also provides some evidence beyond the application benchmark for the utility of triangle multiplication.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is limited: Pairmixer is essentially a removal-based simplification of Pairformer using an already established primitive. Related systems such as MiniFold and Genie2 already demonstrate triangle-multiplication-centric architectures, so the main novelty is validating this design at scale for general cofolding rather than introducing a fundamentally new method.

The claim of matching state-of-the-art predictors across folding and docking benchmarks is too broad. On CASP15, Pairmixer is materially below the retrained or public Pairformer on several interaction metrics—for example, DockQ success is 0.52 versus 0.64/0.68, and ligand lDDT is 0.34 versus 0.36/0.45. Several CASP subsets are also extremely small, with only 12–14 applicable complexes.

Most comparisons use oracle selection over five samples. Pairmixer has no confidence model, and its reported first-sample result is not directly comparable to confidence-ranked top-1 predictions from other systems. This limits the evidence for practical end-to-end parity.

The binder-design section establishes speed and memory benefits but not design quality: it supplies only a single qualitative visualization and no quantitative structural, sequence-diversity, confidence, experimental-binding, or success-rate evaluation. Thus the claim that BindFast produces comparable designs is insufficiently supported.

Memory scalability is a central motivation, yet the paper reports only a few OOM thresholds rather than peak-memory curves across sequence lengths, batch sizes, and sampling configurations. Runtime reporting also omits important reproducibility details such as precision, compilation/kernel settings, warm-up procedure, and variance across repeated measurements.

Statistical uncertainty is not reported for most architecture comparisons and ablations. Small differences are repeatedly described as matching or surpassing without paired significance tests or confidence intervals, making it difficult to distinguish genuine equivalence from evaluation noise.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical bottleneck in AlphaFold3-style cofolding systems and proposes a strikingly simple architecture: retaining pair representations and triangle multiplication while removing triangle attention and sequence updates.

The empirical study is unusually broad and compute-intensive. It includes multiple model scales, training curves, matched Pairformer and sequence-only Transformer baselines, RCSB and CASP15 evaluations, several biomolecular modalities, distogram/contact analysis, recycling sensitivity, and component/mixer ablations.

The efficiency improvements are practically meaningful: Pairmixer uses substantially fewer training GPU-days and FLOPs and achieves inference speedups that increase with sequence length, reaching roughly 4x at 2,048 tokens.

Pairmixer generally remains close to the matched Pairformer across the main structure-prediction metrics. The results support the useful conclusion that explicit pair representations and triangle multiplication account for much of Pairformer's predictive capability.
The paper is clear, well organized, and provides extensive architectural, FLOP, training, and hyperparameter details.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is limited: the principal method is the removal of existing Pairformer components. The paper provides little theoretical justification for why triangle multiplication should replace triangle attention beyond their shared triplet structure and empirical performance.

The claim that removed modules are unnecessary or redundant is stronger than the evidence. The direct ablation in Table 6 shows that removing triangle attention degrades performance under the tested schedule, and the paper's explanation that additional training recovers performance complicates the claimed training-efficiency advantage. A compute-matched study that disentangles architecture, optimization speed, depth, and convergence would be more convincing.

The main evaluations use five-sample oracle selection, which is not representative of deployment and can obscure differences in sample quality. Pairmixer has no trained confidence model, so its reported first-sample result is not directly comparable to confidence-ranked top-1 predictions from other systems. Comparisons to AlphaFold3 and Chai-1 are also imported from prior work rather than run within one controlled pipeline.

Results on the small CASP15 interaction subsets are mixed: Pairmixer is often below the matched Pairformer, with only 12-14 applicable ligand or interface examples for several metrics. The manuscript consequently overstates the evidence for broad parity across interaction types.

The binder-design application demonstrates runtime and memory benefits but does not evaluate design success quantitatively. Two qualitative structures are insufficient to establish that BindFast preserves binding quality, sequence quality, diversity, or experimental success, so claims about enabling biologically relevant binder design remain preliminary.

The implementation changes both the backbone and the MSA module by removing triangle attention, making it difficult to attribute observed accuracy and efficiency differences specifically to the proposed Pairmixer backbone. A factorial ablation of these two changes is missing.

Statistical uncertainty is not reported for most matched-model tables and ablations. Several differences presented as parity are around one or a few percentage points, which could be meaningful on small benchmarks, while training appears to use only one run per configuration.

The evaluation would benefit from clearer disclosure of structural-date cutoffs, possible overlap with distillation data, per-example paired significance tests, peak-memory measurements across sequence lengths, and direct wall-clock comparisons under multiple hardware and batching settings.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/6f7b87e0a4754db69d3569117543e6b4/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a simple, practically important architectural contribution: removing triangle and sequence attention while retaining triangle multiplication and pairwise feed-forward processing.

The central efficiency claim is supported convincingly: Pairmixer reduces large-model training from 421 to 269 GPU-days, provides 1.6× to 4× inference speedups depending on sequence length, and substantially extends the feasible sequence length in binder-design workloads.
The evaluation is unusually broad, covering RCSB and CASP15 benchmarks, protein-ligand docking, antibody-antigen complexes, protein-nucleic-acid complexes, RNA structures, and multiple model scales.

Controlled comparisons against a retrained Pairformer show near-parity across the main RCSB metrics, while training curves and equal-budget experiments demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoff rather than merely a smaller final model.

The paper includes useful ablations of sequence updates, triangle attention, triangle multiplication, alternative mixers, representation widths, diffusion depth, recycling, and distogram quality. These analyses support the conclusion that explicit pair representations and triangle multiplication are the key ingredients.

The downstream BindFast application demonstrates concrete practical value, with more than 2× faster optimization and successful execution on targets for which the Pairformer version exhausts 80 GB of GPU memory.

The presentation is clear, technically detailed, and includes hyperparameters, FLOP accounting, dataset construction information, sample sizes, and uncertainty intervals for major system-level comparisons.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily architectural simplification rather than a fundamentally new operation: triangle multiplication is inherited from existing AlphaFold-style systems, and the main finding is that other Pairformer components can be removed after sufficient training.

The CASP15 results are less uniformly favorable than the RCSB results. Pairmixer trails the corresponding Pairformer substantially on several interaction metrics, especially DockQ, although the relevant CASP15 subsets are very small.

Much of the main evaluation uses oracle selection over five generated poses. Pairmixer lacks a trained confidence model, so its reported first-pose result is not directly comparable to confidence-ranked top-1 predictions from competing systems and understates an important deployment limitation.

The binder-design evidence establishes runtime and memory improvements but not design quality convincingly: it consists mainly of qualitative structures, without established in-silico success criteria, diversity analyses, or experimental validation.

The mechanistic conclusion that triangle multiplication learns sparse long-range interactions is suggestive rather than definitive. Post-hoc inference-time masking can reveal sensitivity to particular activations, but does not by itself establish the claimed computational mechanism.

Pairmixer retains cubic asymptotic complexity and a quadratic pair representation, so it improves constants substantially without resolving the fundamental scaling bottleneck for very large complexes.
